\chapter{Sixteen to Nineteen, Counting Down}
\label{ch:mw-teens-to-nineteen}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say and write sixteen to nineteen in Marwadi, count one to twenty straight through, and say why nineteen is built on twenty rather than on nine.}

One to twenty run four ways, with the four new signs written against the numbers that needed them, and the subtractive nineteen named and explained.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ḷa]{\mw{ळ} — the letter Hindi does not have}

\label{lesson:MW-W38-lla}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{igyārā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lāvo}, the bring-request verb — \textbf{R4}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{caudā} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a second l}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ळ}} — \emph{ḷa} — the retroflex l
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mw{ल}} has been in the hand since chapter 7. \textbf{\mw{ळ}} is a second l made with the tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth, and it is a real difference in Marwari, not a spelling variant.

It is worth knowing whose letter this is. Standard Hindi has no \textbf{\mw{ळ}}; Marwari, Marathi, Gujarati, Rajasthani more widely and the southern languages all do. A page with \textbf{\mw{ळ}} on it is announcing that it is not Hindi.

Sixteen is the number that needs it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{ळ}} three times. Write \textbf{\mw{ल}} beside it and say which one curls the tongue back. Say both aloud twice, listening for the difference rather than looking for it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The second of the four signs the teens ask for.

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[soḷā]{Hear \emph{soḷā} — sixteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-hear-sola}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{ळ}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{terā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{लावो}} — \textbf{R4}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{चौदा}} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{soḷā} — \textbf{sixteen}
\end{quote}

Six is \emph{chha}. Sixteen is \emph{soḷā}, and the two share nothing you can hear — the teens have worn their small numbers down further here than anywhere else in the set.

What they do share is the retroflex \textbf{ḷ} you have just written. Curl the tongue back for it: \emph{so-ḷā}, not \emph{so-lā}. This is where the new letter earns its lesson.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[soḷā]{\mw{सोळा} — sixteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-sola}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{soḷā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{चौदा}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chāy lāvo} — \textbf{R4}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{pandarā} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{सो}} + \textbf{\mw{ळा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} — \emph{soḷā} — sixteen
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mw{सो}} is already a word in this book: a hundred. Sixteen is that syllable with \textbf{\mw{ळा}} after it — which is why the retroflex letter had to come first.

Write \textbf{\mw{सो}} and \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} one above the other. Two signs apart, a hundred and sixteen.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} once while looking. Write \textbf{\mw{सो}} above it and \textbf{\mw{ल}} below it, then say which of the three lines is the hundred and which letter is the one Hindi does not have.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\mw{अ} — the vowel that has no mark}

\label{lesson:MW-W38-a}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{पंदरा}}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{चाय} \mw{लावो}} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the vowel with no mark at all}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{अ}} — \emph{a} — the short vowel every bare consonant already says
\end{quote}

Every other vowel in this book arrived twice: as a mark and as a standing letter. \textbf{\mw{अ}} is different, and the difference is the point of the lesson. Its mark is \emph{nothing at all} — a consonant written plain, \textbf{\mw{क}}, is already read \emph{ka}. That is why you have written this vowel a thousand times without ever seeing it.

When a word \emph{begins} on that sound there is no consonant to hide inside, so the letter has to appear. \textbf{\mw{आ}}, isolated in chapter 2, is its long partner: the same shape with one upright added.

Eighteen is what needs it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{अ}} three times. Write \textbf{\mw{आ}} beside it and mark the one stroke that makes the vowel long. Then write \textbf{\mw{क}} and say what vowel is already in it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The third of the four signs.

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[satarā]{Hear \emph{satarā} — seventeen}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-hear-satara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{अ}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pandarā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the five requests in a row — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{satarā} — \textbf{seventeen}
\end{quote}

Seven is \emph{sāt}. Seventeen is \emph{satarā}, and this is the clearest one in the whole set: \textbf{\mw{सात}} is still visible inside it, with only its long vowel shortened before the \textbf{-arā} ending arrives.

If you have been listening for the shape rather than learning the words, this is the one that proves the shape works.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[satarā]{\mw{सतरा} — seventeen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-satara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{satarā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{ळ}} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the exchange \textbf{dikhāvo — karo — lo — do — lāvo} once — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{स}} + \textbf{\mw{त}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{सतरा}} — \emph{satarā} — seventeen
\end{quote}

Write \textbf{\mw{सात}} and then \textbf{\mw{सतरा}} underneath it. The difference is one mark: the \textbf{\mw{ा}} of seven is gone, and \textbf{\mw{रा}} is added.

That is the whole spelling, and it is the tidiest evidence in the set that the teens are built rather than learned.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{सात}}, then cover it and write \textbf{\mw{सतरा}} from memory. Compare them letter by letter and name the single mark that differs. Then write \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} above both and read the three down the page.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aṭhārā]{Hear \emph{aṭhārā} — eighteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-hear-athara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{सतरा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{soḷā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the six-turn numbered exchange once — \textbf{R3}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{aṭhārā} — \textbf{eighteen}
\end{quote}

Eight is \emph{āṭh}. Eighteen is \emph{aṭhārā}: the same two sounds, with the length moved from the front of the word to the middle of it.

Say them back to back — \emph{āṭh}, \emph{aṭhārā} — and hear the long vowel change places. Eighteen is the second of the two teens that begin on a vowel, which is why the letter came before it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aṭhārā]{\mw{अठारा} — eighteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-athara}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aṭhārā} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{अ}}, four lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{सोळा}} — \textbf{R2}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{अ}} + \textbf{\mw{ठा}} + \textbf{\mw{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} — \emph{aṭhārā} — eighteen
\end{quote}

Here is the standing \textbf{\mw{अ}} doing the one thing it exists for. Write \textbf{\mw{आठ}} and \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} one above the other:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mw{आठ}} opens on the long \textbf{\mw{आ}};
  \item \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} opens on the short \textbf{\mw{अ}}, and moves the length onto \textbf{\mw{ठा}}.
\end{itemize}

Two letters that differ by one stroke, at the front of two numbers ten apart. This is the pair most worth writing twice.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{आठ}}, cover it, write \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} from memory, then uncover and compare the first letter of each. Say which is long and which is short.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\mw{उ} — the last standing vowel}

\label{lesson:MW-W38-u}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{ळ}}, and say which language does not have it — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{अ}} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इ}} — \textbf{R3}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the fifth standing vowel}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{उ}} — \emph{u} — the vowel that hangs under a consonant, standing up
\end{quote}

Since chapter 13 the hand has hooked \textbf{\mw{ु}} beneath a letter, and since chapter 6 the longer \textbf{\mw{ू}}. Neither can begin a word.

\textbf{\mw{उ}} is the fifth vowel this book has had to stand up — after \textbf{\mw{आ}}, \textbf{\mw{ई}}, \textbf{\mw{ए}} and \textbf{\mw{अ}} — and it is the last one the numbers ask for. Nineteen needs it, and nineteen is the last of the teens.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{उ}} three times. Write \textbf{\mw{ु}} under a consonant beside it and say which of the two can open a word. Then write the five standing vowels in a row — \textbf{\mw{अ} \mw{आ} \mw{इ} \mw{ई}} and \textbf{\mw{उ}} — and say each aloud.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The fourth and last of the signs the teens ask for.

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ughaṇīs]{Hear \emph{ughaṇīs} — nineteen}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-hear-ughanis}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{उ}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{satarā}, five lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{igyārā} — \textbf{R3}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ughaṇīs} — \textbf{nineteen}
\end{quote}

Every other teen has been the small number plus an ending. This one is not.

Nine is \emph{no}, and there is no \emph{no} in \emph{ughaṇīs}. What is in it is \textbf{-ṇīs}, which is \emph{bīs}, \textbf{twenty}, worn down — and \emph{ugha-}, which means \textbf{one short of}. So nineteen in Marwari is not \textquotedblleft{}nine-and-ten\textquotedblright{}. It is \textbf{one less than twenty}, and it is built on the number \emph{above} it.

That is why twenty was taught before the teens rather than after them. A course that counted straight up would have printed \emph{bīs} inside nineteen before it had taught \emph{bīs}. The language counts down here, so the book did too.

Turner records the same habit further up: \emph{ekuṇcālīs}, one short of forty, for thirty-nine.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ughaṇīs]{\mw{उघणीस} — nineteen on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C38-ughanis}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ughaṇīs} before you look at it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aṭhārā}, four lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{सतरा}} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{इग्यारा}} — \textbf{R3}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{उ}} + \textbf{\mw{घ}} + \textbf{\mw{णी}} + \textbf{\mw{स}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{उघणीस}} — \emph{ughaṇīs} — nineteen
\end{quote}

Four pieces and no new sign: \textbf{\mw{उ}} from the last lesson, \textbf{\mw{घ}} from chapter 10, the retroflex \textbf{\mw{ण}} from chapter 4, and \textbf{\mw{स}} from the first page of the book.

Write \textbf{\mw{बीस}} under it. The \textbf{\mw{ीस}} at the end of nineteen is the \textbf{\mw{ीस}} of twenty, with a retroflex \textbf{\mw{ण}} in front of it instead of \textbf{\mw{ब}}. What the ear was told, the page shows.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\mw{उघणीस}} once while looking, then write \textbf{\mw{बीस}} beneath it and ring the \textbf{\mw{ीस}} in both. Finish by writing \textbf{\mw{अठारा}} above the pair, so eighteen, nineteen and twenty stand in a column.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{One to twenty, and the number that counts backwards}

\label{lesson:MW-R38-count-twenty}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{उघणीस}} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\mw{अठारा}}, four lessons back — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the five-turn counter exchange, with no figures in it — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
The count is complete for the first time. Run it four ways.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Say one to twenty straight through, out loud, once slowly and once fast.
  \item Hear six of the twenty named out of order; say each back and say the one above it.
  \item Write four of the nine teens from dictation.
  \item Write the four signs this run of numbers added — \textbf{\mw{इ}}, \textbf{\mw{ळ}}, \textbf{\mw{अ}}, \textbf{\mw{उ}} — and beside each write the number that needed it.
\end{enumerate}

Then answer aloud: which of the twenty is not built on a smaller number, and what is it built on instead?
